df['totalwgt_lb'] = df.birthwgt_lb + df.birthwgt_oz / 16.0
agepregcontains the mother’s age at the end of the pregnancy. In the data
file,agepregis encoded as an integer number of centiyears. So the first line
divides each element ofagepregby 100, yielding a floating-point value in
years.
birthwgt_lbandbirthwgt_ozcontain the weight of the baby, in pounds
and ounces, for pregnancies that end in live birth. In addition it uses several
special codes:
97 NOT ASCERTAINED
98 REFUSED
99 DON'T KNOW
Special values encoded as numbers aredangerousbecause if they are not
handled properly, they can generate bogus results, like a 99-pound baby.
Thereplacemethod replaces these values withnp.nan, a special floatingpoint value that represents “not a number.”
As part of the IEEE floating-point standard, all mathematical operations
returnnanif either argument isnan:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.nan /

def CleanFemPreg(df):
df.agepreg /= 100.0

na_vals = [97, 98, 99]
df['birthwgt_lb'] = df.birthwgt_lb.replace(na_vals, np.nan)
df['birthwgt_oz'] = df.birthwgt_oz.replace(na_vals, np.nan)

Most doctors recommend induced labor if a pregnancy exceeds 42 weeks,
so some of the longer values are surprising. In particular, 50 weeks seems

The best way to handle outliers depends on “domain knowledge”; that is,
information about where the data come from and what they mean. And it
depends on what analysis you are planning to perform.
In this example, the motivating question is whether first babies tend to be
early (or late). When people ask this question, they are usually interested in
full-term pregnancies, so for this analysis I will focus on pregnancies longer
than 27 weeks.
